title: About
text:
I am Karuna Reddy, an academic at the University of Auckland, where I work as a Professional Teaching Fellow in Data Science at the School of Computer Science, and also serve as Deputy Director of Data Science. I coordinate courses and supervise Masters and PhD students on research and industry projects.
My research is in survey sampling methodology, with a focus on optimal stratification, mathematical programming and optimisation, along with broader interests in data science and machine learning. I did my BSc, MSc and PhD at the University of the South Pacific (USP) in Fiji, and before Auckland, I was a Lecturer in Data Science at USP, and prior to that, I was a Research Fellow in Survey Statistics at the Australian National University (ANU) in Canberra.
On this blog I share the R packages I build, such as stratifyR, FitVerse, clusta and multistrata, with worked examples and notes on the methods behind them. I hope it is of good use to you, and I look forward to hearing from you if you have any comments or questions on any of these R libraries.

title: multistrata
text:
Multivariate Optimum Stratification and Sample Allocation
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      remotes::install_github("karunaredz/multistrata")
stratifyR finds optimal boundaries for surveys stratified on a single variable. In practice, many surveys stratify on two or more variables at the same time and need to estimate several study variables well. multistrata extends stratifyR to that general case.
It jointly determines boundaries and sample allocation across multiple stratification variables and multiple study variables, minimising a weighted composite variance objective. The algorithm alternates between a boundary update and an exact generalised Neyman allocation, embedded in a multi-start scheme to avoid poor local solutions.

title: multistrata
text:
Quick Start
library(multistrata)

# simulate a two-variable population
set.seed(42)
pop <- sim_population(N = 5000, p = 2, q = 2, scenario = "independent")

# joint stratification on X1 and X2, estimating Y1 and Y2
res <- stratify_multi(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),          # 3 strata per variable = 9 total strata
  n_total    = 500,
  omega      = c(0.5, 0.5),      # equal weight on both study variables
  n_starts   = 50
)
print(res)
summary(res)
H_vec gives the number of strata for each stratification variable. With H_vec = c(3, 3) you get a 3x3 grid of 9 strata in the joint space.

title: multistrata
text:
Core Function: stratify_multi()
The main function takes your population frame, your study variables, and a strata grid. It returns optimal boundaries, stratum sample sizes, and diagnostics.

Key arguments
stratify_multi(
  data,                    # stratification variables (N x p data frame or matrix)
  study_vars,              # study (target) variables (N x q)
  H_vec,                   # strata per variable, e.g. c(3, 3) or c(4, 2, 3)
  n_total,                 # total sample size
  omega      = NULL,       # study-variable weights (default: equal)
  constraint = "n_total",  # "n_total" or "cost"
  cost_total = NULL,       # budget C* (when constraint = "cost")
  cost_fixed = 0,          # fixed overhead deducted from budget
  cost_per_unit = 1,       # per-unit cost (scalar or H-vector)
  cv_targets = NULL,       # max CV per study variable, e.g. c(0.03, 0.03)
  distributions = NULL,    # NULL (empirical) or "auto" or named list of families
  method     = "cobyla",   # boundary solver: "cobyla" or "slsqp"
  n_starts   = 50,         # number of random starts
  n_min      = 2,          # minimum sample per stratum
  verbose    = FALSE,      # print per-start progress
  trace      = FALSE       # store per-iteration objective sequence
)






TipReproducibility



The multi-start scheme draws its initial boundaries at random. Always set a seed before any design you intend to report.
set.seed(1)
res <- stratify_multi(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(4, 3), n_total = 600)

title: multistrata
text:
Two Weight Modes
The stratum weights Wh (the fraction of the population in each stratum) can be estimated in two ways.

  
    Empirical mode (default)
    Wh is the sample proportion of units falling in each stratum. Uses only the data, no distributional assumptions. Set distributions = NULL.
  
  
    Parametric mode
    Wh is computed from marginal CDF differences under a fitted distribution. Set distributions = "auto" for AIC-based family selection, or supply families directly.
  

Auto mode picks the best-fitting marginal family per stratification variable:
res <- stratify_multi(
  data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500,
  distributions = "auto"
)
# res$.meta$distributions shows the selected families
You can also supply families directly:
dists <- list(
  X1 = list(family = "lnorm", meanlog = 1.2, sdlog = 0.8),
  X2 = list(family = "gamma", shape = 2.5, rate = 0.4)
)
res <- stratify_multi(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500,
                      distributions = dists)
Supported families: norm, lnorm, gamma, exp, weibull, beta, unif, chisq, t, cauchy, logis, pareto, triang. When FitVerse is installed, auto mode can also search its 52 families.

title: multistrata
text:
Two Solvers

  
    COBYLA (default)
    method = "cobyla"Derivative-free constrained optimisation. Works in both empirical and parametric modes. Robust and fast for most problems.
  
  
    SLSQP
    method = "slsqp"Gradient-based solver using the closed-form weight gradient (Section 4.2 of the paper). Parametric mode only. Faster convergence when a good distribution fit is available.
  


Checking the solution
After fitting, check the quality diagnostics:
res$objective        # optimal composite variance Phi*
res$optimality_gap   # gap above the lower bound (0 = at the bound)
res$kkt_residual     # first-order stationarity residual
res$kkt_ok           # TRUE if residual is below tol_kkt
res$converged        # did the solver converge within max_iter?
res$n_starts_run     # number of random starts completed

title: multistrata
text:
Reading the Results
res$boundaries       # list of p boundary vectors (one per stratification variable)
res$allocation       # stratum sample sizes (integer vector of length H_total)
res$stratum_stats    # per-stratum N_h, W_h, n_h, A_h, within-stratum variances
The print method shows a formatted summary:
print(res)
================================================
  Multivariate Optimum Stratification (multistrata)
================================================
  Stratification variables : 2  (X1, X2)
  Study variables          : 2  (Y1, Y2)
  Strata per variable      : 3 x 3
  Total strata             : 9
  ...
  Composite variance (Phi) : 0.0048
  Optimality gap           : 0.12%
  Converged                : YES
  Multi-starts used        : 50

title: multistrata
text:
Precision-Driven Design: find_n()
The usual question is “given n, what is the best design?”. Sometimes the question runs the other way: “what is the smallest n that keeps all CVs below a target?”. find_n() answers that.
fn <- find_n(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  cv_targets = c(0.03, 0.03),     # max 3% CV on Y1 and Y2
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_starts   = 20
)
print(fn)
# fn$n          -- smallest feasible total sample size
# fn$allocation -- stratum sizes at that n
# fn$cv_achieved -- actual CVs achieved
It works by integer bisection over the CV-constrained allocation sub-problem. Boundaries are fixed from a single optimisation run and reused, which keeps the computation fast.

title: multistrata
text:
Choosing the Strata Grid: choose_H()
More strata always reduce variance, but the gains level off. choose_H() traces the optimal composite variance across a family of candidate grids and flags the elbow.
ch <- choose_H(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  n_total    = 500,
  H_each     = 2:5,       # tries 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, 5x5
  n_starts   = 10,
  plot       = TRUE
)
ch$table            # Phi*, optimality gap, relative gain per grid
ch$recommended      # recommended H_vec (elbow)
The plot shows the Phi* curve with the recommended grid marked. Go beyond the recommended grid only if the additional precision is worth the operational cost of more strata.

title: multistrata
text:
Priority Trade-Off: omega_sweep()
When you have two study variables and do not know how to weight them, omega_sweep() shows how the optimal design changes as the priority shifts from one to the other.
sw <- omega_sweep(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_total    = 500,
  n_grid     = 11,           # 0%, 10%, ..., 100% weight on Y1
  n_starts   = 10
)
plot(sw)
The plot traces Phi* and per-variable variance against the weight on Y1. The flat middle region, if there is one, shows where the design is robust to the exact choice of weights.

title: multistrata
text:
Cost-Constrained Design
When sampling units in different strata cost different amounts, supply a per-stratum cost vector and a total budget instead of a fixed n.
res_cost <- stratify_multi(
  data          = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars    = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec         = c(3, 3),
  constraint    = "cost",
  cost_total    = 50000,
  cost_fixed    = 2000,         # fixed overhead (travel, setup)
  cost_per_unit = c(rep(20, 5), rep(40, 4)),   # H_total = 9 strata
  n_starts      = 30
)
The cost-aware design adjusts both boundaries and allocation. Strata with high per-unit costs get fewer units and the boundaries may shift to rebalance.

title: multistrata
text:
CV-Constrained Allocation
Specify maximum acceptable coefficients of variation for each study variable instead of (or alongside) a total sample size.
res_cv <- stratify_multi(
  data       = pop[, c("X1", "X2")],
  study_vars = pop[, c("Y1", "Y2")],
  H_vec      = c(3, 3),
  n_total    = 800,
  cv_targets = c(0.05, 0.04),   # 5% CV on Y1, 4% on Y2
  n_starts   = 30
)
res_cv$cv_achieved    # CVs actually achieved by the optimal allocation

title: multistrata
text:
Design Without Data: stratify_multi_density()
You can plan a stratified sample before collecting data, using assumed marginal distributions from a past survey or pilot study.
dists <- list(
  X1 = list(family = "lnorm", meanlog = 1.8, sdlog = 0.7),
  X2 = list(family = "gamma", shape = 3.0,   rate  = 0.5)
)
res_dens <- stratify_multi_density(
  distributions = dists,
  H_vec         = c(3, 3),
  n_total       = 400,
  omega         = c(0.5, 0.5)
)
Stratum weights are computed from the marginal CDFs. Study-variable moments come from Gauss-Kronrod quadrature of the marginal densities. This matches the empirical mode in the large-sample limit.
The three planning tools have density-mode twins, so the whole planning workflow runs with no data at all: find_n_density() for the smallest sample meeting a precision target, choose_H_density() for the strata grid, and omega_sweep_density() for the priority trade-off. benchmark_density_designs() compares the density design against the simpler rules. Each takes the same distributions list as stratify_multi_density() in place of a data frame.
fn <- find_n_density(distributions = dists, cv_targets = c(0.03, 0.03),
                     H_vec = c(3, 3))
ch <- choose_H_density(distributions = dists, n_total = 400, H_each = 2:5)

title: multistrata
text:
Survey Integration
Two functions take the optimal design into production.

assign_strata()
Applies the boundaries from a fitted design to any set of units: an estimation frame, a fresh census extract, or hold-out data.
# fit on a pilot sample, score the full frame
strata_labels <- assign_strata(res, newdata = full_frame[, c("X1", "X2")])
table(strata_labels)
The function matches columns by name when available, so you do not need to worry about column order.


as_svydesign()
Exports a survey::svydesign object ready for estimation with the survey package or srvyr.
svy <- as_svydesign(res, frame = pop)
# standard survey estimation from here
library(survey)
svymean(~Y1 + Y2, design = svy)

# or just a labelled frame for srvyr
labelled_frame <- as_svydesign(res, frame = pop, frame_only = TRUE)
# columns .stratum, .N_h, .n_h, .weight are added automatically

title: multistrata
text:
Visualisation

Boundary DiagramInteractive 3-D (rgl)Allocation Bar ChartWeights Bar ChartOmega Sweep


plot_strata(res)
For one stratification variable: density with boundary walls. For two variables: a 3-D perspective plot of the joint density with boundary planes. The same function works for any number of variables.


plot_strata_rgl(res)
For two stratification variables, plot_strata_rgl() draws the same joint density and boundary planes as a rotatable 3-D scene you can spin with the mouse. It needs the rgl package. Good for presentations and for getting a feel for where the cut planes sit.


plot(res, which = "allocation")
Bar chart of stratum sample sizes. Shows how the allocation spreads across strata.


plot(res, which = "weights")
Stratum weights Wh as a bar chart. Useful for checking how uniformly the population is distributed across strata.


sw <- omega_sweep(data, study_vars, H_vec = c(3, 3), n_total = 500)
plot(sw)
Traces the precision trade-off as the weight shifts between two study variables.

title: multistrata
text:
Benchmarking
benchmark_designs() compares the multistrata design against simpler alternatives: proportional allocation, equal allocation, and two classical boundary rules (Dalenius-Hodges and Gunning-Horgan).
bm <- benchmark_designs(res, pop)
print(bm)
Results show composite variance and per-variable CVs for each design at the same total sample size.

title: multistrata
text:
Simulated Populations
sim_population() generates test populations with known structures.
pop <- sim_population(N = 5000, p = 2, q = 2, scenario = "independent")
Available scenarios:







Scenario
Description




"independent"
Stratification and study variables uncorrelated


"correlated"
Moderate positive correlation between X and Y variables


"weibull_pareto"
Heavy-tailed establishment-survey archetype


"copula"
Dependent stratification variables via a Gaussian copula with log-normal margins

title: multistrata
text:
Built-in Datasets
The package also ships three ready-made example populations, so you can try every function here without any data of your own. All three are fictitious but built to look like real survey frames, each with two stratification variables and two or three study variables.









Dataset
Setting
Stratification variables
Study variables




pacific_agri
Pacific agricultural survey
land area (lognormal), labour (gamma)
crop yield, livestock value, expenditure


business_survey
Business turnover survey
employees (lognormal), assets (Pareto)
turnover, wage bill


health_survey
Health survey
age (beta), BMI (normal)
systolic blood pressure, cholesterol



data(pacific_agri)
res <- stratify_multi(
  pacific_agri[, c("land_area", "labour_units")],
  pacific_agri[, c("crop_yield", "livestock_value", "expenditure")],
  H_vec = c(4, 3), n_total = 600, omega = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)
)
The business_survey frame has a heavy Pareto tail on assets, which is the classic case where a take-all top stratum and careful boundaries matter most.

title: multistrata
text:
Shiny App
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "DT", "plotly"))   # once
run_app()
The app exposes the full workflow without writing code:

Data input: upload your own CSV, generate a simulated population, or use one of the three built-in datasets
Design: set H_vec, n_total or budget, solver, weight mode, and omega
find_n: enter CV targets, get the minimum n
choose_H: scan candidate grids and view the elbow
Omega explorer: slide the priority weight and watch the design change
Benchmark: compare against proportional, equal, and classical rules
Visualise: boundary diagram, allocation bar chart, cost surface
Export: download report (PDF/HTML) and a reproducible R script with the set.seed() call

The generated R script includes the exact set.seed() call for the run shown on screen, so the design can be reproduced from the console.

title: multistrata
text:
Who Is multistrata For?

  🏛 National Statistical OfficesBusiness and agricultural surveys that stratify on size and sector simultaneously, with precision targets on multiple indicators.
  📐 Survey MethodologistsA reproducible, open implementation with formal convergence guarantees, optimality gaps, and KKT diagnostics for peer review.
  🔬 Applied ResearchersHealth, agricultural, economic, and environmental studies where more than one stratification variable is available at the design stage.
  📊 Planning-Stage DesignUse the density mode and find_n() to plan a complete survey before collecting data, from distributional assumptions alone.
  🎓 Teachers and StudentsThe Shiny app and sim_population() make the concepts of joint stratification and the Neyman trade-off easy to explore.

title: multistrata
text:
Helper and Diagnostic Functions
Alongside the main design functions, the package exports a set of smaller building blocks. You rarely need them for a standard design, but they are useful for custom work, for checking a result by hand, and for teaching.

  neyman_alloc()Generalised Neyman allocation for a fixed set of strata. The exact inner step the optimiser uses, exposed on its own.
  variance_lower_bound()The Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound on the composite variance at a set of boundaries. The basis of the optimality gap.
  composite_variance()The weighted composite variance of any design you supply, so you can score a design that did not come from the optimiser.
  design_cv()The achieved coefficient of variation for each study variable under a given design.
  relative_efficiency()The efficiency of one design against another at the same sample size.
  compute_stratum_stats_parametric()Per-stratum weights and moments from fitted marginals, the parametric-mode engine behind the objective.
  fit_distributions()Fit and AIC-rank the candidate marginal families for each stratification variable, the same step that auto mode runs.

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Optimal Survey Stratification in R
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("stratifyR")  ·  remotes::install_github("karunaredz/stratifyR")
When your survey variable is continuous, like income, farm production, or claim size, you can cut its range into bands and sample from each band separately. The tricky part is deciding where the cuts should go, how many units to take from each band, and whether the precision gain is worth the effort.
stratifyR 2.1-0 works all of that out for you. One call gives you the optimal boundaries, the sample size per stratum, and a plain-language efficiency report.

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Quick Start
library(stratifyR)
data(sugarcane)   # 13,894 cane growers in Fiji

# 4 strata · total sample 500 · Dynamic Programming solver
res <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "dp")
summary(res)
One call fits the best distribution, finds optimal boundaries, and allocates the sample. The summary shows one row per stratum with the boundaries, weight, variance, and allocation.
New in 2.1-0, simple functions take the results out for you, so you never need to know how the result is stored:
boundaries(res)            # optimal stratum boundaries
allocation(res)            # one row per stratum: Nh, Wh, Sh, WhSh, nh and fh
objective(res)             # objective function, sum of Wh*Sh (lower = better)
variance(res)              # variance of the estimated mean, with the finite population correction
fitted_distribution(res)   # fitted distribution and its parameters

s <- summary(res)          # a summary object; print it when you want to see it
as.data.frame(s)           # the summary table as a data frame

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Distribution Fitting Step
Before placing any boundaries, strata.data() automatically fits your variable’s distribution from these candidates:
Normal · Log-Normal · Gamma · Weibull · Exponential · Cauchy · Uniform · Pareto · Triangular · Right-Triangular
The fitted distribution is used by the Dynamic Programming solver to compute each stratum’s contribution exactly. Since 2.0-3 the Pareto and triangular fits work properly inside the package, and the Pareto likelihood is computed in a numerically stable form.






Tip



Already know the distribution? Use strata.distr() to supply it directly. No data needed (see Design Without Data).

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Four Solvers

  
    Dynamic Programming
    method = "dp"The default. Globally optimal on a fine grid for the fitted distribution, followed by a short local refinement that can only improve the answer.
  
  
    EXACT
    method = "exact"Dynamic programming on the data themselves. Returns the best possible partition of your sample. Exact for up to 20,000 distinct cut points.
  
  
    COBYLA
    method = "cobyla"Fast multi-start solver. One start comes from a quick coarse exact search, so it copes well with very skewed data. Best for interactive use.
  
  
    GLOBAL
    method = "global"Two phases: a broad DIRECT-L search on the rank scale, then a local refinement. A safe, fast choice for skewed data.
  

dp   <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "dp")
ex   <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "exact")
cob  <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "cobyla")
glob <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500, method = "global")

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
section: Full Variance and a Take-All Stratum
text:
Full Variance and a Take-All Stratum
The usual objective, the sum of \(W_h S_h\), ignores the finite population correction, and Neyman allocation can ask for more units than a stratum holds. Both matter when your sample is a large part of the population, or when a few very large units sit at the top of the range, as in many business and farm surveys.
The exact solver has two options for these cases:
# minimise the full variance, including the finite population correction
fv <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500,
                  method = "exact", fpc = TRUE)

# also let the top stratum be sampled completely (a take-all stratum)
ta <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500,
                  method = "exact", takeall = TRUE)

c(default = variance(ex), fpc = variance(fv), takeall = variance(ta))
summary(ta)   # shows the take-all stratum, if one is chosen
With fpc = TRUE the minimum is certified when the bound is reached. With takeall = TRUE every size of take-all stratum is tried together with the other boundaries. variance() is computed from the final allocation, so you can compare the designs directly and keep the smallest.






TipWhen to use it



If n/N is not small, or the top stratum looks over-allocated, use method = "exact", takeall = TRUE. In our benchmark of 65 settings it gave the smallest achieved variance every time, in about 12 seconds in median.

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Visualising the Design

2D Density Plot3D Cost SurfaceBoundary Explorer


Histogram with fitted density curve and colour-coded strata shading. Immediately shows where the boundaries fall and how the data mass is split.
plot(res)


Interactive plotly surface showing how the objective function changes as boundaries move. Reveals that the optimum sits in a well.
plot(res, type = "3d")


One slider per interior boundary. Drag it and the objective function updates in real time. Good for teaching and for checking how sensitive the design is to small boundary changes.
plot(res, type = "interactive")

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Design Efficiency Report
cd <- compare_designs(res)
cd
Compares three designs at the same sample size: Simple Random Sampling, Proportional Allocation, and Optimal Neyman Allocation. For each: variance, standard error, design effect, equivalent SRS size, and percentage saving.






NoteReading the report



The equivalent SRS size tells you how many units a simple random sample would need to match the precision of your stratified design. On skewed data such as the sugarcane production, it is many times larger than the stratified sample.

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Choosing the Number of Strata
More strata always lower the objective function, but the gains level off quickly. Scan a range and look for the elbow:
for (L in 2:6) {
  r <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = L, n = 500, method = "cobyla")
  cat("L =", L, "  objective =", round(objective(r), 2), "\n")
}
The Shiny app does this automatically and marks the recommended stratum count on the curve.

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Design Without Data
You can plan the full design before any fieldwork using an assumed distribution from a past round or pilot study:
# Household income survey: log-normal, 20,000 units, n = 1,000
g <- strata.distr(h = 4, initval = 500, dist = 119500,
                  distr = "lnorm",
                  params = c(meanlog = 9.616, sdlog = 0.703),
                  n = 1000, N = 20000, method = "dp")
allocation(g)
compare_designs(g)

title: stratifyR 2.1-0
text:
Cost-Constrained Allocation
When sampling costs differ by stratum (large units cost more to visit):
ch <- c(20, 30, 50, 80)   # cost per sampled unit, stratum 1 to 4

cost_res <- strata.data(sugarcane$Production, h = 4, n = 500,
                        method = "dp", cost = TRUE, ch = ch)
allocation(cost_res)
The cost-aware design adjusts both the boundaries and the allocation, and moves more of the sample into the cheaper strata, so the same total n costs less in the field. Its variance is a little higher than the Neyman design’s, so it is the better choice when the budget, rather than the sample size, is fixed.

title: FitVerse 1.0-3
text:
Parametric Distribution Fitting in R
    
      
      
      
      
    
    
      install.packages("FitVerse")  ·  library(FitVerse)
Figuring out which distribution fits your data can take a while. Is it Gamma or Log-Normal? Maybe Weibull? Trying them one at a time is tedious, and eyeballing a histogram only gets you so far.
FitVerse does the searching for you. Give it your data and it fits every distribution family that suits the chosen method, estimates the parameters by MLE, MOM or L-moments, ranks the fits, runs four goodness-of-fit tests, and returns a clean summary with plots. One line of code.
Version 1.0-3 is now on CRAN. The source code is on GitHub at https://github.com/karunaredz/FitVerse.

title: FitVerse 1.0-3
text:
Core Workflow

Quick Start
library(FitVerse)

# Built-in precip data: average annual precipitation in 70 US cities
x <- as.numeric(precip)

# Fit every family by MLE and rank the fits by AIC
fit <- fitverse(x, xlab = "Annual precipitation (inches)")

head(ranking(fit)[, c("Rank", "Distribution", "Method", "AIC", "Delta_AIC", "KS_p", "AD_p")], 5)
#  Rank          Distribution Method      AIC Delta_AIC   KS_p   AD_p
#     1                 Dagum    MLE 564.7508    0.0000 0.4423 0.5683
#     2                  PERT    MLE 565.7535    1.0027 0.1349 0.2269
#     3      Truncated Normal    MLE 566.2037    1.4529 0.2060 0.1311
#     4     Generalised Gamma    MLE 566.5333    1.7825 0.3460 0.4548
#     5 Exponentiated Weibull    MLE 566.7180    1.9672 0.3368 0.4421






NoteWhat happens in one call



fitverse() fits every family that supports the chosen method, estimates the parameters, ranks the fits by AIC, runs four goodness-of-fit tests, and draws a two-panel diagnostic plot.




Key Arguments
fitverse(x,
  dists       = "all",    # a subset, e.g. c("gamma", "lognormal", "gev"), or "all"
  method      = "MLE",    # "MLE", "MOM", "LMOM", or several, e.g. c("MLE", "LMOM")
  criterion   = "AIC",    # ranking criterion: "AIC" or "BIC"
  xlab        = "x",      # axis label for plots and reports
  plot        = TRUE,     # draw the diagnostic plot?
  interactive = FALSE,    # interactive plotly version? (needs plotly)
  top_n       = 3,        # number of density curves to overlay
  verbose     = TRUE)     # print the results to the console?


Working With the Result
ranking(fit)          # ranked table of all fitted models
coef(fit)             # best-fit parameter estimates
fit$best_fit          # best fit: parameters, log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, GoF tests
fit$all_fits          # every fitted model
fit$data_summary      # n, mean, sd, skewness, kurtosis, range


S3 Methods

print(fit): best-fit distribution, parameters and GoF tests
summary(fit): data summary, best fit and the top ten models
plot(fit): two-panel diagnostic plot
ranking(fit): full ranking table
coef(fit): best-fit parameter vector
logLik(fit)   AIC(fit)   BIC(fit)
as.list(fit)   to_json(fit): for use in other tools and web apps
save_plot(fit, "fig.pdf", dpi = 600): save the plot to a file

title: FitVerse 1.0-3
text:
Diagnostic Plot
Every call draws a two-panel diagnostic plot by default.
Left panel (density): a histogram with the top top_n fitted density curves overlaid. The best-fit distribution is highlighted and its PDF formula is shown on the figure.
Right panel (Q-Q plot): theoretical quantiles of the best-fit distribution against the sample quantiles. Points close to the diagonal mean a good fit.
# Interactive version (needs plotly)
fit <- fitverse(x, interactive = TRUE)

# Save without displaying
save_plot(fit, file = "precipitation_fit.png", dpi = 600)
save_plot(fit, file = "precipitation_fit.pdf")   # PNG, PDF or SVG by extension






TipL-Moment Ratio Diagram



For hydrological and extreme-value work, use the L-moment ratio diagram as an exploratory tool before fitting. It plots the sample L-skewness and L-kurtosis against the theoretical curves of several families.
lmrd(x)

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Spectral, Distribution-Aware and Dynamic-Programming Clustering
    
      
      
      
    
    remotes::install_github("karunaredz/clusta")
Clustering often begins with a simple question: which observations belong together? The answer becomes less simple when groups form rings, crescents, spirals, or ordered segments. A single method is rarely suitable for all of these settings.
We developed clusta to bring several related clustering tools into one R package. The common idea is to use dynamic programming when observations can be represented on an ordered axis. On that axis, the package can search all valid contiguous partitions and find the best boundary placement for the chosen objective. For multivariate data, clusta provides several ways to construct or use such an ordering.
The package’s main multivariate method is S-MPDP, short for Spectral Mathematical Programming Dynamic Programming clustering. S-MPDP uses a neighbourhood graph to unfold complex cluster shapes into a one-dimensional signal. It then fits a distribution to that signal and places cluster boundaries by dynamic programming.
This article gives a practical tour of version 1.0-1. It begins with the simplest one-variable problem, moves to non-convex multivariate data, and ends with diagnostics, benchmarking, data, figures, and the Shiny app.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Install and load the package
Install the development version from GitHub:
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("karunaredz/clusta")
library(clusta)
The core package uses fitdistrplus. Other packages are suggested rather than required. They add the Shiny app, ggplot2 figures, some validation measures, additional benchmark methods, and the optional FitVerse distribution engine.
# Optional tools used in later sections
install.packages(c(
  "shiny", "bslib", "ggplot2", "DT", "cluster", "clue",
  "mclust", "dbscan", "mlbench"
))
You can see the package guides at any time:
vignette("clusta", package = "clusta")
vignette("smpdp", package = "clusta")
help(package = "clusta")

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Start with one variable
Suppose the data contain three groups along a single measured variable. Here the natural clusters are contiguous intervals. The default wcss method finds the partition that minimises the total within-cluster sum of squares.
set.seed(123)
x <- c(
  rnorm(60, mean = 0,  sd = 0.8),
  rnorm(60, mean = 6,  sd = 1.0),
  rnorm(60, mean = 13, sd = 1.2)
)

fit_1d <- clusta(x, k = 3)
fit_1d
summary(fit_1d)
plot(fit_1d)
For one variable, the dynamic program searches the complete set of contiguous three-group partitions. The result is therefore the global minimum of the stated WCSS problem. The printed object reports cluster sizes, centres, WCSS, BIC, silhouette width, and the optimality statement.
head(fit_1d$cluster)
fit_1d$boundaries
fit_1d$tot.withinss
fit_1d$gap_pct
gap_pct = 0 certifies a global optimum for the WCSS problem. A nonzero value is a certified upper bound based on the package’s lower bound. It can be conservative.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
One interface, nine methods
The clusta() function gives access to nine methods. If method is omitted, the package uses wcss for one variable and projection for multivariate data.

  ONE VARIABLEwcssFinds the globally optimal contiguous partition under within-cluster sum of squares.
  ONE OR MORE VARIABLESprojectionUses PC1, a supplied direction, or a supplied score. It then solves the one-dimensional WCSS problem exactly on that score.
  ESTIMATION VARIANCEestvarUses an exact dynamic program on one variable or a projection score. Objectives include Neyman, Gaussian, and WCSS costs.
  DISTRIBUTION AWAREparametricFits a distribution by AIC and places model-based boundaries by dynamic programming on a numerical grid.
  NON-CONVEX DATAspectralRuns S-MPDP. A spectral graph representation is compressed to one signal, then partitioned by the distribution-aware dynamic program.
  TWO VARIABLESexact2dFor exactly two variables and k = 2. It enumerates separating directions and certifies the full-space WCSS optimum.
  TWO VARIABLESsweepSearches separating directions for any k. It is global for k = 2 and finds the best parallel-line partition for k greater than 2.
  ORDERED ROWSsequenceFinds the exact multivariate segmentation along a known order, such as time, distance, or a transect.
  GRAPH HEURISTICgraphBuilds a Euclidean minimum spanning tree and removes edges greedily to reduce WCSS. It is a useful heuristic, not an exact graph partition.

These methods do not make the same optimality claim. For example, projection is exact after the projection has been chosen, not in the original multivariate space. S-MPDP is exact for its Stage 2 boundary problem on the fitted one-dimensional signal, not for every possible partition of the original data. Keeping this distinction clear is important when reporting results.

Projection for several variables
fit_iris <- clusta(
  iris[, 1:4],
  k = 3,
  method = "projection",
  scale = TRUE
)

fit_iris
plot(fit_iris)
You may supply your own direction or score when the scientific problem already provides a meaningful order.
fit_direction <- clusta(
  iris[, 1:4],
  k = 3,
  method = "projection",
  direction = c(1, 0, 0, 0)
)


Distribution-aware boundaries
The parametric method first fits a distribution to the variable or projection score. The default engine compares Normal, Log-Normal, Gamma, Weibull, and Exponential families when their supports are suitable. It selects by AIC and places boundaries by minimising the fitted model’s total \(W_hS_h\) cost on a numerical grid.
set.seed(321)
y <- c(rgamma(120, shape = 2, rate = 1),
       rgamma(80, shape = 7, rate = 0.8))

fit_parametric <- clusta(y, k = 3, method = "parametric")
fit_parametric$distr
fit_parametric$fit_params
plot(fit_parametric)
If the optional FitVerse package is installed, fit_engine = "fitverse" searches its larger family collection. fit_engine = "best" tries both engines and keeps the boundary set with the lower empirical \(W_hS_h\) value.
fit_wide <- clusta(
  y,
  k = 3,
  method = "parametric",
  fit_engine = "fitverse",
  fit_dists = "all"
)

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
S-MPDP for non-convex clusters
K-means is useful when groups are compact and roughly spherical. It is poorly matched to two moons, concentric rings, or intertwined spirals because those groups cannot be separated well by nearest-centre regions. S-MPDP takes a different route.

  1. Build a local graphConstruct a locally scaled k-nearest-neighbour graph. The default mutual rule keeps an edge only when each point selects the other.
  2. Unfold the dataUse the normalised Laplacian, its leading eigenvectors, row normalisation, and PCA to produce one ordered signal.
  3. Fit the signalCompare candidate distributions by AIC and retain the best supported model for the spectral signal.
  4. Place boundariesUse dynamic programming to select the Stage 2 boundaries and map the resulting labels back to the original observations.


A two-moons example
moons <- gen_two_moons(n = 500)
X <- moons[, c("x", "y")]

smpdp_fit <- spectral_mpdp(
  X,
  h = 2,
  k_neighbors = 15,
  mutual = TRUE
)

smpdp_fit
summary(smpdp_fit)
The dedicated spectral_mpdp() interface returns an object of class smpdp. Its main table contains the original features, the spectral score, the assigned cluster, and an assignment-confidence value.
head(smpdp_fit$cluster_results)
table(smpdp_fit$cluster_results$cluster)
The same method is also available through the common interface:
fit_common <- clusta(
  X,
  k = 2,
  method = "spectral",
  k_neighbors = 15
)
Use spectral_mpdp() when you want all six S-MPDP figures and the Stage 1 and Stage 2 details. Use clusta(..., method = "spectral") when you want the common clusta object and its S3 methods.


Read the graph checks
k_neighbors is the main S-MPDP tuning setting. Small values keep the graph local, but may leave isolated points or too many connected components. Large values connect more of the data, but can blur local geometry.
Every S-MPDP result reports the number of graph components and isolated observations. Treat a connectivity warning as part of the analysis. It usually means that k_neighbors should be increased, or that the union graph should be examined with mutual = FALSE.
union_fit <- spectral_mpdp(X, h = 2, k_neighbors = 15, mutual = FALSE)
The mutual and union rules answer slightly different graph questions. It is better to report which rule was used than to switch between them without explanation.

title: clusta 1.0-1
section: Six views of an S-MPDP result
text:
Six views of an S-MPDP result
The package provides six matching base R and ggplot2 views.
plot(smpdp_fit, "clusters")
plot(smpdp_fit, "signal")
plot(smpdp_fit, "confidence")
plot(smpdp_fit, "eigengap")
plot(smpdp_fit, "similarity")
plot(smpdp_fit, "profile")
The cluster map uses the two original variables when there are exactly two. For higher-dimensional data, it displays the first two principal components. The signal plot shows where Stage 2 placed the boundaries. The confidence plot highlights observations close to a boundary. The similarity plot helps you inspect graph block structure, while the profile plot compares standardised feature means across clusters.
ggplot2::autoplot(smpdp_fit, "clusters")
ggplot2::autoplot(smpdp_fit, "signal")
ggplot2::autoplot(smpdp_fit, "profile")
For an ordinary clusta object, use plot() for base graphics or fviz_clusta() for a ggplot2 figure.
plot(fit_iris, "clusters")
plot(fit_iris, "silhouette")
fviz_clusta(fit_iris, type = "clusters")

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Choosing the number of clusters

Spectral eigengap guide
suggest_k() examines the graph spectrum. It is a guide rather than a formal decision rule.
k_guide <- suggest_k(X, k_neighbors = 15, k_max = 8)
k_guide
plot(k_guide)


Diagnostic scan over k
clusta_elbow() fits a selected method over a range of cluster counts. It returns WCSS, BIC, average silhouette width, and the available optimality-gap value.
k_scan <- clusta_elbow(x, k_range = 1:8, method = "wcss")
Look for agreement among the graph spectrum, WCSS elbow, BIC, silhouette, scientific knowledge, and cluster interpretability. A single index should not decide the analysis on its own.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Sensitivity and bootstrap stability

Sensitivity to h and k_neighbors
The results should not depend on one unexamined tuning choice. smpdp_sensitivity() runs a grid of neighbourhood sizes and cluster counts. With known labels it reports ARI and NMI as well as silhouette. Without labels it uses silhouette for the printed summary.
sensitivity <- smpdp_sensitivity(
  X,
  truth = moons$class,
  k_grid = c(8, 10, 15, 20, 30),
  h_grid = 2:4,
  mutual = TRUE,
  seed = 12345
)

sensitivity
plot(sensitivity, metric = "ARI")


Bootstrap Jaccard stability
cluster_stability() resamples the observations, refits S-MPDP, and matches each original cluster to the closest bootstrap cluster by Jaccard overlap.
stability <- cluster_stability(
  X,
  h = 2,
  k_neighbors = 15,
  B = 25,
  seed = 12345
)

stability
plot(stability)
The function reports a score for each cluster and an overall mean. A high mean is reassuring, but it does not replace inspection of individual clusters. A single weak cluster can be hidden by a good overall average.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Evaluate a clustering
cluster_metrics() accepts the feature matrix, optional true labels, and predicted labels. It returns eight measures in a fixed order.
pred <- smpdp_fit$cluster_results$cluster
scores <- cluster_metrics(X, true_labels = moons$class, pred_labels = pred)
scores








Measure
Interpretation
Preferred direction




ARI
Agreement with known classes, adjusted for chance
Larger


NMI
Shared information between classes and clusters
Larger


Silhouette
Cohesion and separation in feature space
Larger


Purity
Majority-class share within clusters
Larger


Accuracy
Best one-to-one matching of clusters and classes
Larger


CH
Between-cluster to within-cluster dispersion
Larger


DB
Within-cluster spread relative to separation
Smaller


Dunn
Minimum separation relative to maximum cluster diameter
Larger



ARI, NMI, purity, and accuracy require known labels. Silhouette, CH, DB, and Dunn use the feature matrix. Silhouette needs the optional cluster package, and accuracy needs clue. Pairwise-distance measures can be expensive on large data, so you can request only the metrics needed.
cluster_metrics(
  X,
  true_labels = NULL,
  pred_labels = pred,
  metrics = c("Silhouette", "CH", "DB")
)
When labels are available, keep them out of the clustering feature matrix. They are for evaluation, not fitting.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Compare methods fairly
run_clustering_benchmarks() returns labels from a selected set of methods on the same feature matrix. Available choices are S-MPDP, K-Means, conventional spectral clustering, HDBSCAN, agglomerative clustering, and optional multi-level spectral clustering through sClust.
predictions <- run_clustering_benchmarks(
  X,
  L = 2,
  k_neb = 15,
  mutual = TRUE,
  seed = 12345,
  methods = c("S-MPDP", "K-Means", "Spectral", "Agglomerative")
)

comparison <- t(vapply(
  predictions,
  function(z) cluster_metrics(X, moons$class, z),
  numeric(8)
))

round(comparison, 3)
HDBSCAN requires dbscan. MSC requires sClust. Optional methods are skipped with a warning when their packages are not installed. HDBSCAN may return noise points, and MSC may return a different final number of groups from the requested maximum. Both facts should be considered when comparing results.
For a study with several datasets, put one score matrix together with datasets in rows and methods in columns. friedman_ranks() ranks the methods within each dataset and reports the Friedman and Iman-Davenport tests.
ari_by_dataset <- rbind(
  data_A = c(`S-MPDP` = 0.86, `K-Means` = 0.51, Spectral = 0.80),
  data_B = c(`S-MPDP` = 0.72, `K-Means` = 0.68, Spectral = 0.70),
  data_C = c(`S-MPDP` = 0.91, `K-Means` = 0.75, Spectral = 0.84)
)

ranks <- friedman_ranks(ari_by_dataset, higher_better = TRUE)
ranks
plot(ranks)

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Data included with clusta
The package contains seven real benchmark datasets and three additional worked or simulated datasets.

  glass214 observations, 9 features, and 6 glass classes.
  breast_cancer569 observations, 30 diagnostic features, and 2 classes.
  raisin900 observations, 7 morphological features, and 2 classes.
  rice3,810 observations, 7 shape features, and 2 classes.
  ceramic88 observations, 17 chemical features, and 2 archaeological groups.
  image_segmentation2,310 observations, 19 image features, and 7 classes.
  waveform5,000 observations, 21 features, and 3 classes.
  v_shapeA stored two-dimensional V-shaped benchmark.
  cassiniA stored two-dimensional Cassini benchmark with 3 classes.
  smpdp_toyA small worked dataset for learning the S-MPDP workflow.

A typical labelled dataset has numeric feature columns and a separate class column.
data(ceramic)
X_ceramic <- ceramic[, setdiff(names(ceramic), "class")]
y_ceramic <- ceramic$class

ceramic_fit <- spectral_mpdp(X_ceramic, h = 2, k_neighbors = 41)
cluster_metrics(X_ceramic, y_ceramic, ceramic_fit$cluster_results$cluster)
Six generators make it easy to explore non-convex shapes and to test code at different sample sizes.
two_moons   <- gen_two_moons(n = 500)
v_data      <- gen_v_shape(n = 400)
circles     <- gen_concentric_circles(n = 1500)
smiley      <- gen_smiley(n = 400)
spirals     <- gen_three_spirals(n = 900, noise = 0.02, cycles = 1.4)
cassini_sim <- gen_cassini(n = 2000)
Each generator returns x, y, and class. The random seed is set inside the generator so that the same call is reproducible.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
Work with the returned objects
The clusta class follows familiar R conventions.

print(fit)   overall result, centres, fit measures, and optimality information
summary(fit)   one row per cluster with size, proportion, WCSS, silhouette, and centres
plot(fit)   cluster or silhouette figure in base R
fitted(fit)   fitted centre for every observation
predict(fit, newdata)   new labels, using the exact separating line for exact2d and nearest centres otherwise
fviz_clusta(fit)   a ggplot2 cluster or silhouette figure

names(fit_iris)
fit_iris$cluster
fit_iris$centers
fit_iris$size
fit_iris$withinss
fit_iris$tot.withinss
fit_iris$bic
fit_iris$avg.silwidth
fit_iris$direction
fit_iris$var_explained
Direct access is useful for reports and tables, but print() and summary() are the safer starting points because they explain the method-specific result.

title: clusta 1.0-1
section: Explore the package in the Shiny app
text:
Explore the package in the Shiny app
The app is included inside the installed package. Install its optional interface packages once, then launch it with:
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "ggplot2", "DT"))
shiny::runApp(system.file("app", package = "clusta"))
The app is designed as an analysis path rather than a gallery. A useful first run is:

Choose a built-in dataset, such as Ceramic, Two moons, or Waveform.
Check the supplied starting values for the number of clusters and neighbourhood size.
Choose the mutual or union graph rule.
Decide whether to compare baseline methods.
Click Run clustering.
Read the overview and graph-health message before moving to the figures.
Inspect the cluster map, spectral signal, confidence, eigengap, similarity matrix, and cluster profiles.
Use the stability, bootstrap, PCA, and dynamic-programming panels when they answer your analysis question.
Export the assignments, metrics, figures, or generated R code.

The benchmark comparison uses the same Run clustering button. There is no separate benchmark button. The selected baseline methods and metrics are applied when the main analysis runs.

Built-in app examples
The app includes Iris, all seven real package datasets, and six simulated shapes. Each built-in choice supplies a tested starting value for h and k_neighbors. For example, Waveform starts with three clusters and k_neighbors = 50.
For large built-in datasets, baseline comparisons are turned off automatically because dense spectral methods and pairwise-distance metrics can take time and memory. You can turn them back on when the comparison is needed.


Upload your own CSV
When uploading a CSV file:

Select the numeric feature columns.
If known labels are present, select the label column separately.
Decide whether to standardise the features.
Check that k_neighbors is smaller than the number of observations.
Run the analysis and read any graph-connectivity warning.

The selected label column is removed from the clustering features, even when the labels are numeric. This prevents the true answer from leaking into the fit. Constant features remain available to the clustering method, but the app omits them from standardised PCA calculations because they have zero variance.
The R code tab is especially useful. It writes a reproducible script that reflects the current controls, so an app analysis can be rerun at the console and shared with collaborators.

title: clusta 1.0-1
text:
A careful analysis workflow
A reliable clustering analysis needs more than a single fitted object. The following sequence works well for many applications:

Clean the feature matrix and deal with missing values before fitting.
Keep known labels separate from the features.
Standardise when variables are measured on very different scales, unless the original scale has a scientific meaning that should be preserved.
Choose a method that matches the structure of the problem.
For S-MPDP, inspect graph components and isolated points.
Study more than one value of h and k_neighbors.
Examine the cluster map, signal, confidence, and profiles together.
Report both internal and external metrics when labels exist.
Check bootstrap stability.
Compare with credible baseline methods.
Save the settings, seed, package version, and exported R code.

This does not guarantee that every cluster is scientifically meaningful. It makes the reasoning visible and the result reproducible.

title: clusta 1.0-1
section: What the package does not claim
text:
What the package does not claim
clusta gives exact solutions in several clearly defined settings, but it does not turn every multivariate clustering problem into a global optimisation result.

wcss is globally optimal for a contiguous partition of one variable.
projection and multivariate estvar are exact on the chosen one-dimensional score.
parametric is optimal on its fitted-model grid for the chosen Stage 2 objective.
exact2d certifies the two-cluster WCSS optimum for exactly two variables.
sweep is global for two clusters and otherwise searches partitions separated by parallel lines.
sequence is exact along the supplied order.
graph is a minimum-spanning-tree heuristic built from Euclidean feature distances. Version 1.0-1 does not use a custom spatial adjacency matrix.
S-MPDP is exact for Stage 2 boundary placement on the fitted spectral signal. It does not claim the global optimum over all partitions of the original multivariate space.

These limits tell the reader exactly what was optimised and help another researcher reproduce the analysis.
